vignette:
Mona, a 77-year-old single Middle Eastern woman who had built much of her identity around being a steady tutor and a calm presence for children in her neighborhood, described the war years as the point at which her life divided into a “before” and an “after.” During shelling near her apartment, she had been caught outside in a stairwell while windows shook and people shouted below, and the scene lodged in her mind with a force she still found humiliating. In the weeks that followed, she began to feel dead inside, as if the part of her that had once been patient, confident, and useful had gone missing. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to think about what happened, she would not be able to handle it, and she spoke about herself with harsh certainty, calling herself weak for not having “moved on” like others seemed to. Those beliefs quietly shaped how she lived: when she took the bus to tutor, she made sure to sit or stand near the exit, scanning where she could leave quickly if she needed to; she avoided television programmes, films, and even newspaper pieces that showed bombed streets, displaced families, or any similar conflict, telling herself she could not afford to let such things into her mind. 

At first these habits felt to Mona like common sense, a way to keep herself composed, but over time they narrowed her world. The closer she stayed to the exit and the more firmly she turned away from anything resembling the war, the more she gave herself the message that she was fragile and unable to cope. That sense of weakness fed back into the same guarded routines, until avoiding reminders became proof, in her own mind, that she really was not strong enough. She noticed that she dwelt on how she used to be before the event — someone who could teach, travel to visit relatives, and watch the news without distress — and the comparison only deepened her shame. Even ordinary moments in her daily life as a tutor could carry the same message; if a classroom door slammed or if she found herself too far from an exit, she immediately felt the old need to position herself where she could escape, as though surviving depended on never being caught unprepared. 

Her memories of the shelling were not distant recollections but experiences that arrived with the same terror she had felt then. Sometimes, without warning, something in her surroundings — a sudden bang from a neighbour’s apartment, the crackle of a radio announcement, the sight of dust drifting in a shaft of light — could bring back the full memory at once. In those moments she did not remember the event so much as re-enter it; her body would tense, and she would feel as though the frightening scene was happening right now rather than years ago. Because she had spent so long steering away from reminders, those intrusions felt even less manageable, as if the memory were waiting just beyond whatever she tried not to see. The more she organised her days around staying near exits and avoiding media, the more isolated her world became, and the more abruptly the memory could seize her when a reminder slipped through. She began to dread the possibility of being flooded by the same terror in public, and this fear reinforced her reluctance to watch anything or think too long about the war.

By the time she sought help, Mona had become troubled by how much of her life was being shaped by these reactions. She continued tutoring, but the effort of sitting near doors, keeping one eye on the room, and steering conversations away from anything related to conflict left her exhausted and detached. She no longer felt like the woman she had been before the war, and that loss of herself weighed heavily alongside the fear that if she opened the door to the memories, she would not be able to contain them. What finally brought her in was the growing sense that the tightening circle of avoidance, shame, and sudden reliving was stealing not only her peace but her remaining confidence, and she hoped, with some caution, that treatment might help her face the memories without being overwhelmed by them.
